transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (TidalWorks CTO), Sara Nguyen (TidalWorks ML Eng), Priya Sharma (TidalWorks Infra)

Auto-generated summary (short):
TidalWorks is evaluating Redwood for a 6-week POC to validate unit economics for an LLM-powered search augmentation feature. Primary success criteria: latency under 250ms p50 for short queries, cost per 1k tokens under target budget, and no PII leakage (SOC2+VPC). Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmark template and cost model; schedule a 2-hour benchmark run; customer to provide sample dataset and traffic profile.

Topics: success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, batching & caching knobs, hosted vs dedicated vs private options, timeline, security needs

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Liam: Yep loud and clear.
[00:05] Aisha: Great. Quick intros, I'll be the AE coordinating the pilot; Miguel is our solutions engineer who will help with the bench- — the benchmark harness. Miguel, quick wave?
[00:14] Miguel: Hi all, morning/afternoon depending where you are.
[00:17] Sara: Sara here, ML eng, mainly doing the model integration work.
[00:19] Priya: Priya, infra. I'll be responsible for access and security.
[00:22] Aisha: Awesome. So high level, TidalWorks wanted to scope a POC to validate cost and latency before committing to a dedicated pool. Today we want to nail down success criteria, what workloads we run, and how we measure per-token costs.
[00:34] Liam: Yeah, we're building a search-augmentation that calls the LLM for re-rank and short answers. Typical prompt lengths are 30-60 tokens, responses 20-80 tokens. Target is sub-250ms p50 for the re-rank path, and our budget is roughly $12k/month for inference for the feature— that's for initial rollout. We want concrete per-1k-token numbers so finance can sign off.
[00:56] Aisha: Makes sense. Quick qual: current stack?
[01:00] Sara: We're on AWS, primarly us-east-1, Kubernetes EKS, internal infra. We host some models ourselves today for dev, but production we want either Redwood hosted or Redwood dedicated in our VPC.
[01:10] Priya: For the VPC option we'd need KMS integration and SAML SSO. Also important: audit logs for every request, and data retention controls.
[01:19] Miguel: Totally. We support KMS/HSM options and SAML; audit logs are included in the private/dedicated offering. Hosted API can be used for quick prototyping but we understand the security asks.
[01:29] Liam: Also curious about batching and caching — we expect a lot of repeated prefixes with re-rank, so KV cache could help. How much savings should we expect?
[01:38] Miguel: Great question. Ballpark: with prefix caching and continuous batching you might see 20–60% token cost reduction depending on repetition and average sequence length. For re-rank specifically, if prompts are short and we can cache shared context, expect the higher end. But CPU/GPU utilization and concurrency patterns affect latency tradeoffs.
[01:55] Sara: How do you model per-token costs for budgeting? We need a simple formula we can put in a spreadsheet.
[02:00] Aisha: We'll send a cost model template. Quick sketch: unit_cost_per_token = (gpu_hour_cost * 3600 / effective_tokens_per_hour) * deployment_multiplier minus caching_savings — it's in the spreadsheet. We'll provide concrete numbers for a few model variants (open models, q8 quantized, etc.).
[02:18] Liam: Can you show an example?
[02:20] Miguel: Sure — imagine using a quantized 13B model on a T4-equivalent: if you do batching of 8 and average token rate is X, per-1k-token effective cost might be $0.50–$1.20 depending on sequence lengths. For a mid-tier A100 runner it drops. We'll capture variants in the template.
[02:39] Priya: For us, predictable throughput is important. If we go with hosted, what's auto-scaling look like? Cold-starts?
[02:45] Miguel: Hosted auto-scale is fast but can have transient cold starts for large KV cache warmup. Dedicated reserved pools give you predictable QPS and lower tail-latency; private VPC is similar but with your network constraints considered.
[02:59] Liam: Ok. Success criteria — we proposed: 250ms p50, p95 under 800ms? And cost per 1k tokens under $X. Does that sound reasonable?
[03:09] Sara: Also quality regression criteria — we need no more than a 2% drop on our evals vs baseline model. We'll supply eval sets.
[03:16] Miguel: Perfect. We'll run latency and token-costs, and also run your evals to check quality drift. We'll flag failure if quality drops more than agreed threshold.
[03:25] Aisha: Timeline — are you aiming for a 6-week POC?
[03:29] Liam: Yes, 6 weeks is ideal. First week: provisioning + sample-run; week 2: baseline benchmarks; week 3-4: optimization (batching, quantization); week 5: extended run; week 6: handoff and finance sign-off.
[03:42] Aisha: Sounds doable. For the benchmarking itself we'll need a 2-hour controlled run to get steady-state unit economics. That will require a reproducible harness — Miguel will help build that.
[03:52] Miguel: I'll put together a containerized runner. Need sample prompts, tokenization rules, and expected QPS distribution. Sara, can you provide a 10k sample prompt set and a traffic histogram?
[04:03] Sara: Yes, we can. We'll anonymize any PII; it's mostly synthetic logs.
[04:07] Priya: Regarding network egress — we have strict egress rules. For a private deployment we need to ensure outbound ports and private link support. Do you support VPC endpoints?
[04:16] Miguel: We support VPC peering and private links for our private offering. For hosted, we do TLS and can provide IP allowlists but not direct VPC peering. We'll include a deployment checklist.
[04:27] Liam: Any red flags on data retention or PII? We can't permit sending raw user messages to third parties.
[04:33] Aisha: Understood. For Dedicated/Private, customer data stays in your VPC or on your dedicated pool; for hosted we offer data deletion policies and can sign an addendum. We'll send the SOC2 report and the DPA.
[04:45] Priya: Good. Also curious about fallbacks — if you can't hit latency SLO, do you have cheaper model fallbacks or regional routing?
[04:52] Miguel: Yes, smart routing can fallback to smaller quantized variants or route to a different region. We can configure automatic fallback policies and A/B rollouts. That will be part of the optimization phase.
[05:03] Sara: On batching knobs — is there a recommended max batch for low-latency paths?
[05:08] Miguel: For sub-250ms p50, small batches of 4–8 depending on GPU and request concurrency are typical. Larger batches increase throughput but hurt p95/p99. We'll explore that during tuning.
[05:19] Liam: Ok can you put together two cost scenarios: conservative and optimized? Conservative assumes no caching and low batching; optimized assumes caching and q8 quantized models.
[05:29] Aisha: Yep. We'll produce both in the spreadsheet. We'll also add sensitivity: traffic growth 2x and 5x.
[05:36] Priya: Regarding observability — we need token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency, and per-request IDs for audit.
[05:43] Miguel: Console exposes token & latency breakdowns, request tracing, and you can export logs to your SIEM. We'll include a sample dashboard screenshot link in the follow-up deck.
[05:52] Liam: Great. Any blockers to starting?
[05:55] Priya: We need a legal NDAs + DPA in place before data is shared. Also, timeframe for Redwood to provide SOC2?
[06:03] Aisha: We'll attach SOC2 and ISO docs in the follow-up. NDA shouldn't be a blocker — legal can route a template.
[06:09] Liam: Cool. Let's map concrete next steps.
[06:12] Aisha: Action recap — Aisha will send template + deck + SOC2 by Friday (2027-02-12). Miguel will prepare the harness and a rough estimate for per-1k-token costs for 3 model profiles. Sara/Priya will provide sample prompts and network constraints. We'll schedule the 2-hour benchmark for wk of 2/15.
[06:31] Sara: One quick question — for the benchmark, do you simulate user think time or do a steady stream?
[06:35] Miguel: We can do both: a steady-state run for unit economics and a bursty run for latency tails. We'll need the histogram to set inter-arrival times.
[06:43] Liam: Sounds good. Anything else?
[06:46] Priya: No, that's it from infra.
[06:48] Aisha: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and the spreadsheet.
[06:51] Liam: Thanks.

References shared: Redwood benchmark template (link: https://redwood-docs.internal/benchmarks/tidalworks-template), security whitepaper (link: https://redwood-docs.internal/security/soc2), benchmark spreadsheet (attached in follow-up).

End of call.
